answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This line is spoken by Stephen Dedalus in Ulysses (1922), in the “Scylla and Charybdis” episode, during the library debate about Shakespeare — the exact wording is confirmed against the original 1922 text.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: —Bosh! Stephen said rudely. A man of genius makes no mistakes. His errors are volitional and are the portals of discovery.
trail: The line occurs in the “Scylla and Charybdis” episode of Ulysses, set in the National Library of Ireland, where Stephen debates Shakespeare's biography with John Eglinton and others — see the 1922 text on Wikisource ↗.

An Oxford University Press blog piece by Joyce scholar Sam Slote traces how this exact line has itself been repeatedly misquoted in public life, including on a 2013 Irish €10 commemorative coin — see “A man of genius makes no mistakes”: Joycean misapprehensions ↗.
Wikiquote's entry for the novel records the same wording and attributes it to Stephen Dedalus in Episode 9 — see Ulysses (novel) on Wikiquote ↗.
source.excerptNote: Stephen's retort to John Eglinton, who had just suggested that Shakespeare's marriage to Anne Hathaway was simply a mistake.
source.rightsNote: Ulysses was first published in Paris in 1922, well before the 1931 cutoff, and its U.S. copyright has since lapsed — the novel is publicly available in full through Project Gutenberg and Wikisource.

author.name: James Joyce
author.heading: About James Joyce
author.bio: James Joyce was an Irish modernist writer best known for Dubliners (1914), A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916), and his landmark novel Ulysses (1922), which reworks Homer's Odyssey across a single day in Dublin. He is regarded as one of the most influential writers of the 20th century.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The quotation itself is genuine and correctly credited to James Joyce — but it is one of the most frequently garbled lines in his work, which makes it worth flagging.

items.who: Popular condensed version: 'Mistakes are the portals of discovery.'
items.why: Widely circulated on quote sites and social media with the crucial qualifier — that this applies specifically to a 'man of genius' and that the errors are 'volitional' — stripped out, changing Stephen's meaning considerably. See the OUP blog on this ↗.

Issued by the Central Bank of Ireland to honor Joyce as part of a European commemorative coin series, the coin quoted a different Joyce line (from the 'Proteus' episode) inaccurately, becoming a well-publicized embarrassment precisely because Joyce is so often misquoted — see NPR's report ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is authentically Joyce's, spoken by Stephen Dedalus in Ulysses — but it is very often trimmed down to 'mistakes are the portals of discovery,' which loses the original's specific claim about genius and volition; see the full text at Wikisource ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line comes from the “Scylla and Charybdis” episode of Ulysses, set in the National Library of Ireland, where Stephen Dedalus holds forth on a theory of Shakespeare's life and marriage. When John Eglinton suggests that Shakespeare's marriage to Anne Hathaway was simply a mistake, Stephen dismisses the idea — genius, he argues, does not make mistakes in the ordinary sense; its apparent errors are chosen, and become the means by which new understanding is reached.

The aphorism has taken on a life well beyond its original context, frequently cited (and just as frequently truncated) as general wisdom about creativity and failure, stripped of the specific claim about genius that gives it its edge in the novel.
context.pull: His errors are volitional and are the portals of discovery.
